You are building an admin product catalog page for an e-commerce team.

The catalog is read-heavy and should feel fast for day-to-day browsing, so avoid re-querying product data on every request.

Admins can trigger a "Sync latest catalog" action from the page when upstream ERP/PIM data changes (pricing, inventory, availability). After submitting, they should be able to continue working immediately, even if the product list is briefly stale.

The expected behavior is that product data is refreshed in the background and becomes up to date shortly after, across any views that depend on the same catalog data.

Implement the sync trigger as a regular HTML form that uses an inline Server Action in the page.
Use the cache tag name `"products"` consistently for catalog caching and invalidation.

In practice, sync jobs can touch thousands of SKUs, so operators prioritize a responsive admin experience and eventual consistency across catalog views over forcing every request to block on freshly recomputed data.

2	title: revalidateTag
3	description: API Reference for the revalidateTag function.
4	---
5	
6	`revalidateTag` allows you to invalidate cached data on-demand for a specific cache tag.
7	
8	This function is ideal for content where a slight delay in updates is acceptable, such as blog posts, product catalogs, or documentation. Users receive stale content while fresh data loads in the background.
9	
10	## Usage
11	
12	`revalidateTag` can be called in Server Functions and Route Handlers.
13	
14	`revalidateTag` cannot be called in Client Components or Proxy, as it only works in server environments.
15	
16	### Revalidation Behavior
17	
18	The revalidation behavior depends on whether you provide the second argument:
19	
20	- **With `profile="max"` (recommended)**: The tag entry is marked as stale, and the next time a resource with that tag is visited, it will use stale-while-revalidate semantics. This means the stale content is served while fresh content is fetched in the background.
21	- **With a custom cache life profile**: For advanced usage, you can specify any cache life profile that your application has defined, allowing for custom revalidation behaviors tailored to your specific caching requirements.
22	- **Without the second argument (deprecated)**: The tag entry is expired immediately, and the next request to that resource will be a blocking revalidate/cache miss. This behavior is now deprecated, and you should either use `profile="max"` or migrate to [`updateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/updateTag).
23	
24	> **Good to know**: When using `profile="max"`, `revalidateTag` marks tagged data as stale, but fresh data is only fetched when pages using that tag are next visited. This means calling `revalidateTag` will not immediately trigger many revalidations at once. The invalidation only happens when any page using that tag is next visited.
25	
26	## Parameters
27	
28	```ts
29	revalidateTag(tag: string, profile: string | { expire?: number }): void;
30	```
31	
32	- `tag`: A string representing the cache tag associated with the data you want to revalidate. Must not exceed 256 characters. This value is case-sensitive.
33	- `profile`: A string that specifies the revalidation behavior. The recommended value is `"max"` which provides stale-while-revalidate semantics, or any of the other default or custom profiles defined in [`cacheLife`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheLife). Alternatively, you can pass an object with an `expire` property for custom expiration behavior.
34	
35	Tags must first be assigned to cached data. You can do this in two ways:
36	
37	- Using the [`next.tags`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/fetch) option with `fetch` for caching external API requests:
38	
39	```tsx
40	fetch(url, { next: { tags: ['posts'] } })
41	```
42	
43	- Using [`cacheTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag) inside cached functions or components with the `'use cache'` directive:
44	
45	```tsx
46	import { cacheTag } from 'next/cache'
47	
48	async function getData() {
49	  'use cache'
50	  cacheTag('posts')
51	  // ...
52	}
53	```
54	
55	> **Good to know**: The single-argument form `revalidateTag(tag)` is deprecated. It currently works if TypeScript errors are suppressed, but this behavior may be removed in a future version. Update to the two-argument signature.
56	
57	## Returns
58	
59	`revalidateTag` does not return a value.
60	
61	## Relationship with `revalidatePath`
62	
63	`revalidateTag` invalidates data with specific tags across all pages that use those tags, while [`revalidatePath`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidatePath) invalidates specific page or layout paths.
64	
65	> **Good to know**: These functions serve different purposes and may need to be used together for comprehensive data consistency. For detailed examples and considerations, see [relationship with revalidateTag and updateTag](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidatePath#relationship-with-revalidatetag-and-updatetag) for more information.
66	
67	## Examples
68	
69	The following examples demonstrate how to use `revalidateTag` in different contexts. In both cases, we're using `profile="max"` to mark data as stale and use stale-while-revalidate semantics, which is the recommended approach for most use cases.
70	
71	### Server Action
72	
73	```ts filename="app/actions.ts" switcher
74	'use server'
75	
76	import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache'
77	
78	export default async function submit() {
79	  await addPost()
80	  revalidateTag('posts', 'max')
81	}
82	```
83	
84	```js filename="app/actions.js" switcher
85	'use server'
86	
87	import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache'
88	
89	export default async function submit() {
90	  await addPost()
91	  revalidateTag('posts', 'max')
92	}
93	```
94	
95	### Route Handler
96	
97	```ts filename="app/api/revalidate/route.ts" switcher
98	import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
99	import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache'
100	
101	export async function GET(request: NextRequest) {
102	  const tag = request.nextUrl.searchParams.get('tag')
103	
104	  if (tag) {
105	    revalidateTag(tag, 'max')
106	    return Response.json({ revalidated: true, now: Date.now() })
107	  }
108	
109	  return Response.json({
110	    revalidated: false,
111	    now: Date.now(),
112	    message: 'Missing tag to revalidate',
113	  })
114	}
115	```
116

1 --- 2 title: use cache 3 description: Learn how to use the "use cache" directive to cache data in your Next.js application. 4 related: 5 title: Related 6 description: View related API references. 7 links: 8 - app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-private 9 - app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents 10 - app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheLife 11 - app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers 12 - app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag 13 - app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife 14 - app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag 15 --- 16 17 The `use cache` directive allows you to mark a route, React component, or a function as cacheable. It can be used at the top of a file to indicate that all exports in the file should be cached, or inline at the top of a function or component to cache the return value. Functions and components that use `use cache` must be async. 18 19 > **Good to know:** 20 > 21 > - To use cookies or headers, read them outside cached scopes and pass values as arguments. This is the preferred pattern. 22 > - If the in-memory cache isn't sufficient for runtime data, [`'use cache: remote'`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-remote) allows platforms to provide a dedicated cache handler, though it requires a network roundtrip to check the cache and typically incurs platform fees. 23 > - For compliance requirements or when you can't refactor to pass runtime data as arguments to a `use cache` scope, see [`'use cache: private'`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-private). 24 25 ## Usage 26 27 `use cache` is a Cache Components feature. To enable it, add the [`cacheComponents`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) option to your `next.config.ts` file: 28 29 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher 30 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 31 32 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 33 cacheComponents: true, 34 } 35 36 export default nextConfig 37 ``` 38 39 ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher 40 /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 41 const nextConfig = { 42 cacheComponents: true, 43 } 44 45 module.exports = nextConfig 46 ``` 47 48 Then, add `use cache` at the file, component, or function level. All functions and components using `use cache` must be async. When used at file level, every exported function becomes a cached function and must also be async: 49 50 ```tsx 51 // File level 52 'use cache' 53 54 export default async function Page() { 55 // ... 56 } 57 58 // Component level 59 export async function MyComponent() { 60 'use cache' 61 return <> 62 } 63 64 // Function level 65 export async function getData() { 66 'use cache' 67 const data = await fetch('/api/data') 68 return data 69 } 70 ``` 71 72 ## How `use cache` works 73 74 ### Cache keys 75 76 A cache entry's key is generated using a serialized version of its inputs, which includes: 77 78 1. **Build ID** - Unique per build, changing this invalidates all cache entries. If [`deploymentId`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/deploymentId) is configured, it overrides the build ID for cache key purposes. 79 2. **Function ID** - A secure hash of the function's location and signature in the codebase 80 3. **Serializable arguments** - Props (for components) or function arguments 81 4. **HMR refresh hash** (development only) - Invalidates cache on hot module replacement 82 83 When a cached function references variables from outer scopes, those variables are automatically captured and bound as arguments, making them part of the cache key. 84 85 ```tsx filename="lib/data.ts" 86 async function Component({ userId }: { userId: string }) { 87 const getData = async (filter: string) => { 88 'use cache' 89 // Cache key includes both userId (from closure) and filter (argument) 90 return fetch(`/api/users/${userId}/data?filter=${filter}`) 91 } 92 93 return getData('active') 94 } 95 ``` 96 97 In the snippet above, `userId` is captured from the outer scope and `filter` is passed as an argument, so both become part of the `getData` function's cache key. This means different user and filter combinations will have separate cache entries. 98 99 > **Good to know:** When a cached function reads [root parameters](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-root-params), only the ones it actually reads become part of its cache key. 100 101 ## Serialization 102 103 Arguments to cached functions and their return values must be serializable. 104 105 For a complete reference, see: 106 107 - [Serializable arguments](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/use-server#serializable-parameters-and-return-values) - Uses **React Server Components** serialization 108 - [Serializable return types](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/use-client#serializable-types) - Uses **React Client Components** serialization 109 110 > **Good to know:** Arguments and return values use different serialization systems. Server Component serialization (for arguments) is more restrictive than Client Component serialization (for return values). This means you can return JSX elements but cannot accept them as arguments unless using pass-through patterns. 111 112 ### Supported types 113 114 **Arguments:** 115 116 - Primitives: `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `null`, `undefined` 117 - Plain objects: `{ key: value }` 118 - Arrays: `[1, 2, 3]` 119 - Dates, Maps, Sets, TypedArrays, ArrayBuffers 120 - React elements (as pass-through only) 121 122 **Return values:** 123 124 - Same as arguments, plus JSX elements 125 126 ### Unsupported types 127 128 - Class instances 129 - Functions (except as pass-through) 130 - Symbols, WeakMaps, WeakSets 131 - URL instances 132 133 ```tsx filename="app/components/user-card.tsx" 134 // Valid - primitives and plain objects 135 async function UserCard({ 136 id, 137 config, 138 }: { 139 id: string 140 config: { theme: string } 141 }) { 142 'use cache' 143 return
{id}
144 } 145 146 // Invalid - class instance 147 async function UserProfile({ user }: { user: UserClass }) { 148 'use cache' 149 // Error: Cannot serialize class instance 150 return
{user.name}
151 } 152 ``` 153 154 ### Pass-through (non-serializable arguments) 155 156 You can accept non-serializable values **as long as you don't introspect them**. This enables composition patterns with `children` and Server Actions: 157 158 ```tsx filename="app/components/cached-wrapper.tsx" 159 async function CachedWrapper({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) { 160 'use cache' 161 // Don't read or modify children - just pass it through 162 return ( 163
164
Cached Header
165 {children} 166
167 ) 168 } 169 170 // Usage: children can be dynamic 171 export default function Page() { 172 return ( 173 174 {/* Not cached, passed through */} 175 176 ) 177 } 178 ``` 179 180 You can also pass Server Actions through cached components: 181 182 ```tsx filename="app/components/cached-form.tsx" 183 async function CachedForm({ action }: { action: () => Promise }) { 184 'use cache' 185 // Don't call action here - just pass it through 186 return
{/* ... */}
187 } 188 ``` 189 190 ## Constraints 191 192 Cached functions execute in an isolated environment. The following constraints ensure cache behavior remains predictable and secure. 193 194 ### Request-time APIs 195 196 Cached functions and components **cannot** directly access runtime APIs like `cookies()`, `headers()`, or `searchParams`. Instead, read these values outside the cached scope and pass them as arguments. 197 198 ### Runtime caching considerations 199 200 While `use cache` is designed primarily to include uncached data in the static shell, it can also cache data at runtime using in-memory LRU (Least Recently Used) storage. 201 202 With the default in-memory handler, runtime cache behavior depends on your hosting environment: 203 204 | Environment | Runtime Caching Behavior | 205 | --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 206 | **Serverless** | Cache entries typically don't persist across requests (each request can be a different instance), or during revalidation. Build-time caching works normally. | 207 | **Self-hosted** | Cache entries persist across requests. Control cache size with [`cacheMaxMemorySize`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/incrementalCacheHandlerPath). | 208 209 For example, in a serverless environment, a cached function shared by two pages executes on each static shell revalidation, whereas in self-hosted or environments with persistent memory, the cached output is reused if it's still fresh. 210 211 If the default in-memory cache isn't enough, consider **[`use cache: remote`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-remote)** which allows platforms to provide a dedicated cache handler (like Redis or KV database). This helps reduce hits against data sources not scaled to your total traffic, though it comes with costs (storage, network latency, platform fees). 212 213 > [!NOTE] 214 > With the default in-memory handler, serverless instances are ephemeral, so entries may not be reused between requests, unlike with `use cache: remote`. Neither caching directive carries over to a new deploy, because the [cache key](#cache-keys) includes the build (or `deploymentId`) ID. 215 > 216 > For data that needs to persist across deploys, use [`unstable_cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/unstable_cache) for non-`fetch` functions or the [`fetch`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/fetch) cache. 217 218 Very rarely, for compliance requirements or when you can't refactor your code to pass runtime data as arguments to a `use cache` scope, you might need [`use cache: private`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-private). 219 220 ### Draft Mode 221 222 When [Draft Mode](/docs/app/guides/draft-mode) is enabled, all cached functions and components re-execute on every request, and results are not saved to the cache. This ensures draft content is always fresh without requiring any changes to your caching code. 223 224 You can read `isEnabled` from [`draftMode()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/draft-mode) inside a `use cache` scope, however, other runtime APIs like `cookies()` and `headers()` are not allowed, even when Draft Mode is active. See [Passing runtime values to cached functions](/docs/app/getting-started/caching#passing-runtime-values-to-cached-functions) for the recommended pattern. 225 226 ```tsx filename="app/components/content.tsx" 227 import { draftMode } from 'next/headers' 228 229 async function Content() { 230 'use cache' 231 232 const { isEnabled } = await draftMode() 233 const url = isEnabled 234 ? 'https://draft.example.com/content' 235 : 'https://production.example.com/content' 236 237 const data = await fetch(url) 238 return
{/* ... */}
239 } 240 ``` 241 242 Calling `enable()` or `disable()` inside a caching directive scope will also throw an error. Draft Mode can only be toggled in [Route Handlers](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route) or [Server Actions](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data). 243 244 ### React.cache isolation 245 246 [`React.cache`](https://react.dev/reference/react/cache) operates in an isolated scope inside `use cache` boundaries. Values stored via `React.cache` outside a `use cache` function are not visible inside it. 247 248 This means you cannot use `React.cache` to pass data into a `use cache` scope: 249 250 ```tsx 251 import { cache } from 'react' 252 253 const store = cache(() => ({ current: null as string | null })) 254 255 function Parent() { 256 const shared = store() 257 shared.current = 'value from parent' 258 return 259 } 260 261 async function Child() { 262 'use cache' 263 const shared = store() 264 // shared.current is null, not 'value from parent' 265 // use cache has its own isolated React.cache scope 266 return
{shared.current}
267 } 268 ``` 269 270 This isolation ensures cached functions have predictable, self-contained behavior. To pass data into a `use cache` scope, use function arguments instead. 271 272 ## `use cache` at runtime 273 274 On the **server**, cache entries are stored in-memory and respect the `revalidate` and `expire` times from your `cacheLife` configuration. You can customize the cache storage by configuring [`cacheHandlers`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers) in your `next.config.js` file. 275 276 On the **client**, content from the server cache is stored in the browser's memory for the duration defined by the `stale` time. The client router enforces a **minimum 30-second stale time**, regardless of configuration. 277 278 The `x-nextjs-stale-time` response header communicates cache lifetime from server to client, ensuring coordinated behavior. 279 280 ## Revalidation 281 282 By default, `use cache` uses the `default` profile with these settings: 283 284 - **stale**: 5 minutes (client-side) 285 - **revalidate**: 15 minutes (server-side) 286 - **expire**: Never expires by time 287 288 ```tsx filename="lib/data.ts" 289 async function getData() { 290 'use cache' 291 // Implicitly uses default profile 292 return fetch('/api/data') 293 } 294 ``` 295 296 ### Customizing cache lifetime 297 298 Use the [`cacheLife`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife) function to customize cache duration: 299 300 ```tsx filename="lib/data.ts" 301 import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' 302 303 async function getData() { 304 'use cache' 305 cacheLife('hours') // Use built-in 'hours' profile 306 return fetch('/api/data') 307 } 308 ``` 309 310 ### On-demand revalidation 311 312 Use [`cacheTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag), [`updateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/updateTag), or [`revalidateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag) for on-demand cache invalidation: 313 314 ```tsx filename="lib/data.ts" 315 import { cacheTag } from 'next/cache' 316 317 async function getProducts() { 318 'use cache' 319 cacheTag('products') 320 return fetch('/api/products') 321 } 322 ``` 323 324 ```tsx filename="app/actions.ts" 325 'use server' 326 327 import { updateTag } from 'next/cache' 328 329 export async function updateProduct() { 330 await db.products.update(...) 331 updateTag('products') // Invalidates all 'products' caches 332 } 333 ``` 334 335 Both `cacheLife` and `cacheTag` integrate across client and server caching layers, meaning you configure your caching semantics in one place and they apply everywhere. 336 337 ## Examples 338 339 ### Caching an entire route with `use cache` 340 341 To prerender an entire route, add `use cache` to the top of **both** the `layout` and `page` files. Each of these segments are treated as separate entry points in your application, and will be cached independently. 342 343 ```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx" switcher 344 'use cache' 345 346 export default async function Layout({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) { 347 return
{children}
348 } 349 ``` 350 351 ```jsx filename="app/layout.js" switcher 352 'use cache' 353 354 export default async function Layout({ children }) { 355 return
{children}

Done. The admin product catalog page is at `/products`, built and verified against this Next.js version's docs (16.3 canary, Cache Components).

**What I built:**

- `next.config.ts` — enabled `cacheComponents: true`, which is required for `'use cache'` and `cacheTag` in this version.
- `lib/catalog.ts` — a `getCatalog()` data accessor marked with `'use cache'` and `cacheTag('products')`. Any view that reads catalog data through this function shares the same cache entry and the same `"products"` tag, so one invalidation covers all of them. It also returns a `loadedAt` timestamp so staleness is observable on the page.
- `app/products/page.tsx` — the catalog page renders the cached product table and a plain HTML `<form>` whose `action` is an inline Server Action. The action calls `requestCatalogSync()` (a stub in `lib/db.js` representing enqueueing the upstream ERP/PIM job) and then `revalidateTag('products', 'max')`.

**The key API decision:** this Next.js version changed `revalidateTag` — the single-argument form is deprecated, and the second argument picks the invalidation semantics. `revalidateTag('products', 'max')` marks the tag stale with stale-while-revalidate behavior: after syncing, admins immediately keep getting the cached (briefly stale) catalog while fresh data is recomputed in the background on the next visit — no request blocks on recomputation. The alternative, `updateTag('products')`, would expire and refresh within the same request (read-your-own-writes), which would make the sync action block on recomputing data for thousands of SKUs — exactly what the operators said they don't want.

**Verification:** `next build` passes (`/products` shows in the route table with the default 15-minute background revalidate, so day-to-day browsing never re-queries per request), and hitting the production server twice returned the identical cached `loadedAt` snapshot, confirming reads are served from cache.
